newsitem.title: TURKEY: Moslem countries set for troubled Erbakan's summit.
newsitem.headline: Moslem countries set for troubled Erbakan's summit.

text.p: Officials from eight Moslem countries gather in Istanbul this weekend for a summit clouded by a welter of problems facing the group's mastermind, Turkey's Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan.

The meeting is set to launch the Developing-Eight (D-8) economic cooperation group, bringing together Bangladesh, Egypt, Indonesia, Iran, Malaysia, Nigeria, Pakistan and Turkey to put trade, industry and financial projects into practice.
But hopes of economic gains among member countries have been overshadowed by doubts over Erbakan's hold on power and foreign criticism of Turkey's military incursion into northern Iraq.
Erbakan, presiding over a crumbling coalition, shrugged off his domestic crisis with flowing rhetoric before the summit.

"The D-8 is the organisation of a new world. It is a turning point in human history, because a new world is being founded. These moves are being made in the name of all humanity," Erbakan told his Islam-based Welfare Party this week.
But others are less enthusiastic than Erbakan, who promised voters to create an Islamic "Common Market" and turn the Turkish republic away from its traditional Western vocation.

Turkey has failed in its efforts to assemble all eight heads of state or government for the final summit day on June 15. The groundwork for that meeting will be prepared by senior officials meeting on June 12-13 and foreign ministers meeting on Saturday.

Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak will not attend the summit, which follows a row between Cairo and Ankara over Turkey's Iraq operation and growing Turkish-Israeli military cooperation. Foreign Minister Amr Moussa will head Egypt's delegation.
Thousands of Turkish troops poured into northern Iraq on May 14 in an anti-guerrilla operation condemned by the Arab League and some of Turkey's neighbours, including Iran.
Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani was expected to attend the summit despite rising tension with Turkey over Iran's alleged support for the rebel Kurdistan Workers Party.

Erbakan visited all D-8 countries except Bangladesh soon after coming to power last June. He fostered economic links with projects such as a $23 billion gas deal with Iran, drawing strong criticism from NATO-member Turkey's Western allies.

Political analysts say the D-8 group, devised as a potential developing world partner to the G-7 group of rich countries, has been ill thought out in Erbakan's haste to strengthen Turkey's links with the Islamic world.

"The D-8 gives the impression of a group which has been founded hurriedly, without investigating adequately the G-7 experience," Istanbul University professor Hasmet Basar wrote in the daily Milliyet.

Domestically, Erbakan's vision of Moslem brotherhood has been reduced to tatters by fierce opposition from the secularist establishment which has brought his 11-month-old coalition to breaking point and prompted him to seek early elections.
Erbakan, facing the possibility of losing power, continued to talk enthusiastically this week about major D-8 projects to build passenger aircraft, helicopters, cars and computers.

Among planned areas of cooperation, Egypt will oversee trade, Turkey will coordinate industry proposals, Pakistan will be responsible for agriculture, Nigeria will oversee energy plans and Indonesia will be responsible for human resources.
Iran will oversee telecommunication projects, Bangladesh will deal with rural development and Malaysia will focus on privatisation, banking and Islamic insurance, or 'takaful'.

Erbakan's chief adviser, Sedat Celikdogan, told Reuters some Moslem countries, in particular Saudi Arabia, had reacted negatively to their absence from the group, but he was upbeat about the group's prospects.
"If these countries reach a slightly more advanced level of development and attain political stability they will become one of the world's important centres of power," Celikdogan said.
